newsitem.title: GREECE: UPDATED PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - OCT 29.
newsitem.headline: UPDATED PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - OCT 29.

text.p: --The national economy and finance ministry is considering changes to the taxation of mutual funds which will lead to lesser charges, sources say. The ministry has decided to abolish the 15 percent tax on returns and impose a 0.5-1.5 percent tax on active mutual funds.

--Meanwhile, Finance Undersecretary George Drys is scheduled to meet with banking and investor representatives to discuss the government's plans to tax state titles and banking products. --The central bank is to announce changes within the next few days to solvency indices and other capital issues for banks, in line with European Union legislation.
--The objective costing system for real estate values will be

expanded to 70 island and border regions. The ministry is also ready to announce a new valuing system for farm land and property in regions not in town planning zones. The system will be applied throughout Greece by the end of the year. --Changes in the taxation regime for imported used cars back on the table. The finance minstry is examining making the special consumer tax on used cars equivalent to that on new cars.

--Lack of planning and the restrictions placed by the convergence programme, as well as strong ideological differences within the ruling party PASOK, have created a picture of political confusion in regards to the shaping of the 1997 budget. A month before the budget is to be tabled in Parliament, the government still appears to not have decided on a unified economic policy.

--The foreign exchange market in Greece is ready to be deregulated. The Bank of Greece considers that forex deposit accounts held by permanent residents can be deregulated as economic conditions have matured and fears of a forex outflow have receded. Also being considered is taxation of forex deposits. Both moves will expand banking choices for Greek residents.

--Stock Exchange bodies fail to agree over responsibilities for supervision and monitoring of bourse activities. --This week will see the government deciding on new taxes - most probably, 10 percent of interest on treasury bills, a real estate tax, and capital gains tax on share transfers of non-listed firms - and heavier rates for existing taxation for the new budget, affecting both wealthy and lower income earners.

--The government prepares to respond to condemnation by brokers and investors over the wave of speculation on the Athens bourse, which cannot be justified by economic developments or by first half returns of listed companies.
--An investigation begins into the National Bank of Greece and ETBA's 30 billion drachma investment in a luxury cruiseship that has yet to be built at the ETBA-run Avlida shipyards.
--Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou is examining possible changes to the embattled objective tax criteria for 1996 and 1997, related to the criteria for self-employed professionals and merchants.
--National Insurance AEGA swallows three subsidiaries to form insurance colossus.
